title: The Cloak and the Iron Cage: Weber from Erfurt to Munich-Schwabing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Erfurt and the House at Charlottenburg

stops.name: Erfurt, the birth on the Karthäuser Mühlsteg
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a house on the Karthäuser Mühlsteg, an address the next century renumbers Juri-Gagarin-Ring 10, Helene Fallenstein bears her first child. The father is a municipal jurist and National Liberal deputy who keeps a political salon and no religion to speak of; the mother keeps a Calvinist severity her husband has no use for. The quarrel between those two temperaments runs through the house and will one day be the son's own quarrel. Erfurt is where Martin Luther matriculated, took the cowl and said his first mass. Weber is born a few streets from those doors and spends his working life explaining what came out of them.
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque on the Erfurt birth house at Juri-Gagarin-Ring 10, formerly Am Karthäuser Mühlsteg 44
sources: Nominatim geocoding of Juri-Gagarin-Ring 10, Erfurt (correcting two conflicting pins in the research pool)

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the removal to the capital's edge
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The family moves west to Charlottenburg, a town of its own beside Berlin, and the boy grows up inside his father's politics rather than beside them. Deputies, jurists and historians come to the house; the talk at table is the National Liberal talk of the new empire, conducted by men who assume the state is theirs to administer. Helene's piety is not welcome in that room. Her son learns early to sit between the two and listen, and to read whatever is on the shelves; at thirteen he gives his parents historical essays on the Roman emperors for Christmas.
suggested_refs: The Weber household at Charlottenburg as a National Liberal salon of the Gründerzeit

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the Kaiserin-Augusta-Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: enrolment year attested; the attested span runs to 1882, and no month is given
stops.campa: Ten years at the Gymnasium, and what his teachers leave behind is the record of a pupil who is bored. He reads Goethe, Kant, Spinoza and Schopenhauer under the desk while the set curriculum proceeds above it, and takes an Abitur his masters consider unearned by effort. The exact school building is not recoverable from the sources reachable here, so the pin marks the district rather than an address. What is recoverable is the habit, and it holds for life: he takes his education somewhere other than where it is being offered to him.
suggested_refs: The Kaiserin-Augusta-Gymnasium, Charlottenburg, and its curriculum in the 1870s
sources: [R] the coordinate is a Charlottenburg-district approximation, not a surveyed school address

stops.name: Heidelberg, matriculation and the Burschenschaft Allemannia
stops.date_confidence: matriculation year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: He comes up to read law at eighteen and does what his father's son is expected to do: joins a duelling fraternity, the Burschenschaft Allemannia, drinks with it, fences with it, and carries the scar afterwards. He also reads theology, history and economics on the side. Heidelberg is a small town of steep streets where Hegel held his first ordinary chair, and he moves through those same streets four times a day between lecture hall, library, fencing ground and lodging. Weber will spend more of his life in it than anywhere else, and will end up buried on the hill above it.
suggested_refs: The Burschenschaft Allemannia Heidelberg and the Mensur scar in the Weber iconography
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Max Weber' ('Weber war Mitglied der Studentenverbindung Burschenschaft Allemannia Heidelberg'; the research pool's 'Corps Suevia' is an error)
Marianne Weber, Max Weber: Ein Lebensbild (1926), at second hand

stops.name: Strasbourg, the year under arms and the Baumgarten house
stops.date_confidence: the 1883-1884 service year is attested; the October start is inferred from the German military calendar
stops.campa: A year of compulsory service in a garrison town annexed from France twelve years earlier: drill by day, lectures at the Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität when the duty roster permits. The education that matters happens in the house of his uncle, the historian Hermann Baumgarten, a liberal of 1848 who thinks Bismarck's empire was bought too cheaply. Against his own father's comfortable National Liberalism the young Weber hears, for the first time, a patriotism that judges the state instead of serving it. He also falls half in love with his cousin Emmy.
suggested_refs: Hermann Baumgarten's household at Strasbourg and the liberal critique of Bismarck

stops.name: Göttingen, the law student in motion
stops.date_confidence: the 1884-1885 Göttingen terms are attested; the month is inferred from the semester calendar
stops.campa: German law students of the period assemble a degree the way a traveller assembles a route, and Weber's runs Heidelberg, Strasbourg, Berlin, Göttingen. Here he works at the law and adds economics and agrarian history, subjects no examiner will ask him about. He is living on his father's money and resents it. The pattern of the next decade is already fixed: he takes on more reading than any single discipline requires, and he will not stop taking it on until a body that cannot keep pace with him stops him.
suggested_refs: The peripatetic legal curriculum of the German universities in the 1880s

stops.name: Berlin, Unter den Linden: the Referendar examination
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He passes the first state examination in law on the fifteenth of May and enters the years of unpaid apprenticeship in the Berlin courts, living in his parents' house at Charlottenburg because he cannot afford to live anywhere else. The university on Unter den Linden is Wilhelm von Humboldt's foundation, built on the proposition that research and teaching are one act. Weber, drafting court documents by day and reading medieval Italian commercial law at night, is about to demonstrate what that proposition costs a man who takes it literally.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität on Unter den Linden, Humboldt's foundation of 1810

stops.name: Berlin, the dissertation on the medieval trading companies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no reachable source gives the date of the defence, so the month defaults to January
stops.campa: The doctorate is taken on the history of medieval commercial partnerships, the commenda and the societas maris of the Italian ports, under Levin Goldschmidt and Rudolf von Gneist. It is legal history already asking an economic question: how does a form of contract make a form of enterprise possible. Secondary accounts frequently give August Meitzen as the supervisor here. Meitzen supervised the habilitation two years later, and the slip is repeated often enough to have got into otherwise careful summaries.
suggested_refs: Zur Geschichte der Handelsgesellschaften im Mittelalter (1889)

stops.name: Berlin, the habilitation and the East Elbian survey
stops.date_confidence: the 1891 habilitation and the 1892 survey are both attested; this stop carries the earlier year, month unrecorded
stops.campa: Roman agrarian history under August Meitzen earns him the habilitation and a Privatdozent's lectern at Berlin. In the same stretch the Verein für Sozialpolitik sends out its questionnaire on agricultural labour east of the Elbe, and Weber writes the report: some nine hundred pages on Junker estates losing their German workers to the cities and replacing them with seasonal Poles. It is the first performance of what he will keep doing: reading a national political crisis out of contract forms and wage rolls.
suggested_refs: Die Lage der Landarbeiter im ostelbischen Deutschland (1892), for the Verein für Sozialpolitik

stops.name: Oerlinghausen, the marriage to Marianne Schnitger
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries his second cousin in her Westphalian hometown on the twentieth of September. She is twenty-three, has read Kant on her own, and will become a jurist and a writer on the legal position of women. The marriage brings money enough to work without a salary and produces no children. Sixty-one years later she is buried in the same grave. Every text of his that survives him passes through her hands first, which means the Weber the twentieth century reads is, in a strict editorial sense, a book she assembled.
suggested_refs: Marianne Weber, Ehefrau und Mutter in der Rechtsentwicklung (1907)
sources: Marianne Weber, Max Weber: A Biography
Wikipedia coordinate for Oerlinghausen, 51°58′00″N 8°40′00″E (correcting a pool figure 8 km east)

segments.name: Freiburg and the Chair of Karl Knies

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, the first chair
stops.date_confidence: appointment year attested; no reachable source gives the semester month
stops.campa: At thirty he gets his first full professorship, in economics, and a house at Schillerstraße 22 on the quiet side of town. He works the way he will work until his body stops him: whole nights, no holidays, every lecture course built from nothing. His inaugural lecture takes up the German farm worker and the eastward advance of Polish labor, the same territory he will keep returning to. He is, by every account including his own, happy here, and he does not notice what the arrangement is costing.
suggested_refs: The Weber residence at Schillerstraße 22, Freiburg-Mittelwiehre
sources: Nominatim geocoding of Schillerstraße 22, Freiburg (correcting a pool figure 1.25 km northwest)

stops.name: Freiburg, the inaugural address on the nation state
stops.date_confidence: the 1895 address is attested; no reachable source gives the month, defaulted here to May
stops.campa: The inaugural lecture is called The Nation State and Economic Policy, and it is brutal. Economics, he tells the faculty, is not a science of human happiness but a political science, and its final standard of value is the permanent power-interest of the German nation. The Polish seasonal labourers of the East Elbian report reappear in it as a threat. Later admirers handle the address at arm's length; Weber never withdraws it. The man who will spend his life warning about the rationalized machine begins by demanding a stronger one.
suggested_refs: Der Nationalstaat und die Volkswirtschaftspolitik, Freiburg inaugural lecture, 1895

stops.name: Heidelberg, the chair of Karl Knies
stops.date_confidence: the call is attested to 1896; no month is given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Heidelberg calls him back to the chair of economics and finance that Karl Knies has vacated, and at thirty-two he is exactly where he intended to be. He takes over Knies's students and Knies's lecture list, a young man stepping directly into an old man's shoes at the university that will define him more than any other. Weber gets two working years here before the collapse. Everything he is remembered for is written afterwards, by a man who can no longer hold a lecture course.
suggested_refs: The chair of Nationalökonomie und Finanzwissenschaft at Heidelberg, held by Karl Knies to 1896

stops.name: Heidelberg, the quarrel with the father
stops.date_confidence: the quarrel and the father's death are attested to 1897; no reachable source gives a day, and the July placement is inferred from the stated interval of weeks before a death on a journey to Riga
stops.campa: Max Weber Sr. comes to visit and treats Helene as he has always treated her. His son, thirty-three years old and a professor, orders him out of the house and takes his mother's side without qualification. The father leaves. Weeks later he dies on a journey to Riga, and there has been no reconciliation and now cannot be one. No source reachable here records the room or the words; the pin marks the city, and not the villa on the Ziegelhäuser Landstraße, which the Webers do not occupy for another thirteen years.
suggested_refs: The 1897 rupture with Max Weber Sr. and its place in Marianne Weber's account of the breakdown

stops.name: Konstanz, the Heilanstalt Konstanzer Hof
stops.date_confidence: the 1898 admission is attested; no month is given, and the pin marks the Konstanz area rather than a located building
stops.campa: The collapse arrives as exhaustion, insomnia and an inability to read, and it does not lift. He is admitted to a nursing institution for nervous illness and begins four years in which lecturing is impossible and writing comes in fragments. The diagnosis of the age is neurasthenia; the regimen is rest, water and no books. Nobody can locate the building now from the reachable record. The interval itself is documented: the most demanding economist in Germany spends it unable to finish a sentence.
stops.quote: [I]ntense worldly activity is recommended as the most suitable means. It and it alone disperses religious doubts and gives the certainty of grace.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 4, written seven years after this admission; the sentence runs in full 'On the other hand, in order to attain that self-confidence intense worldly activity is recommended as the most suitable means'
suggested_refs: The Heilanstalt für Nervenkranke 'Konstanzer Hof' and the neurasthenia regime of the 1890s

stops.name: Corsica, the first journey south
stops.date_confidence: the Corsican travels fall within an attested 1899-1903 span; the earliest year of that span is carried here and no month is recorded
stops.campa: The doctors send him south, and the Webers begin the pattern of the next four years: Mediterranean light, long walks, no obligations, and the slow discovery that he can think again when nobody expects him to. Corsica is the first of these destinations. No reachable source names the town, so the pin marks the island. Travel is doing for him what the institutions could not, and the itinerary it produces, Corsica and Rome and Florence, will be repeated for more than a decade after he no longer needs it medically.
suggested_refs: The Weber Mediterranean itineraries, 1899-1913
sources: [R] destination named without a town; the coordinate is an island-level reconstruction

stops.name: Bad Urach, the sanatorium under the limestone
stops.date_confidence: the 1900 stay is attested to the year; no month is given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A second institution, this one in a spa town under the cliffs of the Swabian Alb, and the same regimen. He resigns nothing formally yet; Heidelberg keeps paying and keeps waiting. Marianne travels with him and handles the doctors, the correspondence and the accounts. These years leave almost no documents of his own. The hole in the bibliography between 1898 and 1903 is the exact shape of the illness. He is thirty-six years old and has published nothing for two years.
suggested_refs: The Bad Urach cure and the sanatorium culture of Wilhelmine Germany

stops.name: Rome, the winter at Via Cicerone
stops.date_confidence: the stay is attested from October 1901 to March 1902; the day of arrival is not given
stops.campa: The Webers take an apartment at Via Cicerone 3 and stay from October to March. He reads in the libraries, walks, and begins working again on his own terms; the great comparative question about religion and economic conduct is forming in a Catholic city, in a man raised between a Calvinist mother and an unbelieving father. The apartment becomes the first place since the collapse where he can sit at a desk for an hour without his own body driving him back out of the chair.
stops.quote: The God of Calvinism demanded of his believers not single good works, but a life of good works combined into a unified system.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 4, written after these Italian years
suggested_refs: The Weber residence at Via Cicerone 3, Rome, winter 1901-1902
sources: martin_luther.journey.json (canonical Rome pin 41.8886, 12.5064, inherited here in place of the address-level 41.9053, 12.4642)

stops.name: Heidelberg, the teaching laid down
stops.date_confidence: the withdrawal is attested to 1903; no month is given
stops.campa: He gives up regular teaching and accepts an honorary professorship, which is a way of saying the university keeps his name and expects nothing further. He is thirty-nine. From here to the end of the war he holds no salaried post and lectures almost never, and in this condition, formally an invalid, he writes the work the twentieth century reads. The Heidelberg years that matter are not the two he spends as a professor. They are the fifteen he spends as a private scholar with no students and no timetable.
suggested_refs: The Heidelberg Honorarprofessur and the German category of the private scholar

stops.name: New York, the landing
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is attested to August 1904; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Marianne and he cross in late summer for the Congress of Arts and Science, and the first thing America hands him is its vertical scale. He is forty and has not worked properly in six years. The three months ahead will be the most sustained physical exertion of his adult life and will break the grip of the illness; he comes home writing. The country he has landed in is the one his argument is about, the place where the Protestant ethic has run its whole course and left the ethic behind it.
suggested_refs: The 1904 Weber crossing and the American notebooks behind Die protestantischen Sekten

stops.name: Chicago, the Union Stock Yards
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to the 1904 trip; the month is inferred from the itinerary and is not given in the sources
stops.campa: He walks the killing floors where cattle enter one end of the building and leave the other as packed meat, each man on the line performing a single cut for the length of a shift. It is rationalization made visible: the division of labour carried to the point where no worker sees the animal whole. Cruelty he expects of an abattoir. What holds him is the calculation, which is the subject of the rest of his working life, and here he watches it run at full scale on live animals rather than on paper.
stops.quote: Man is dominated by the making of money, by acquisition as the ultimate purpose of his life.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 2
suggested_refs: The Union Stock Yards, Chicago, in 1904, two years before Sinclair's The Jungle

stops.name: St. Louis, the Congress of Arts and Science
stops.date_confidence: the congress convenes in September 1904; no reachable source gives the day of Weber's paper
stops.campa: In Forest Park, on the grounds of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, he reads a paper on rural society in Germany to an international congress assembled around a world's fair. It is his only formal academic appearance in the United States and his first lecture of any kind in six years, delivered in the middle of the American trip that will feed directly into the Protestant Ethic essays. He travels on afterward through the country's cities and farms, taking notes that outlast the paper itself.
suggested_refs: Congress of Arts and Science, Universal Exposition, St. Louis, 1904, published proceedings

stops.name: Indian Territory, the land auctions near Muskogee
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to the 1904 trip; the month is inferred from the itinerary and is not given in the sources
stops.campa: Three years before Oklahoma becomes a state he watches allotted land change hands at auction, and mission schools teaching the children of the people whose land it was. What he is after is the point at which a frontier stops being a frontier: the moment custom becomes title, title becomes market, and the market is the only thing left standing. Within a decade the record of what stood here before will survive mainly as a mission register and a deed book. That is a form of rationalization too, and he notices it.
suggested_refs: Dawes Act allotment and the land auctions of Indian Territory before statehood in 1907

stops.name: Tuskegee, the institute of Booker T. Washington
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to the 1904 trip; the month is inferred from the itinerary and is not given in the sources
stops.campa: He visits the Alabama institute where Booker T. Washington teaches trades to the children of people born into slavery, and he asks his own question rather than the schooling question. The American colour line interests him as a case of status honour maintained without law: caste produced by custom in a republic that has abolished the legal grounds for it. He goes home with the material for essays on race and religion in the postbellum South that he never fully writes, and the notes are absorbed into the sociology of status groups.
suggested_refs: Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in 1904; Weber's later correspondence with W. E. B. Du Bois

stops.name: Mount Airy, the Fallenstein cousins in Carolina
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to the 1904 trip; the month is inferred from the itinerary and is not given in the sources
stops.campa: In the North Carolina hills he finds relatives of his mother's family who emigrated and stayed German and Protestant, and he watches a baptism in a cold creek and a congregation deciding by vote whether a man is fit to be admitted. Membership in the sect, he sees, is a certificate of character the local bank will accept. Out of this visit comes The Protestant Sects and the Spirit of Capitalism, the essay in which the argument of the book acquires a living witness instead of a documentary one.
stops.quote: In the field of its highest development, in the United States, the pursuit of wealth, stripped of its religious and ethical meaning, tends to become associated with purely mundane passions, which often actually give it the character of sport.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 5
suggested_refs: Die protestantischen Sekten und der Geist des Kapitalismus (1906)

stops.name: Heidelberg, the Protestant Ethic in the Archiv
stops.date_confidence: the two parts appear in the 1904 and 1905 volumes of the Archiv; January 1905 is a placeholder for the completed publication
stops.campa: The two parts appear in the journal he now co-edits, and the argument runs like this: the Calvinist doctrine of election left believers no way to know their own fate and no priest to ask, so methodical worldly work became the only available evidence of grace, and the discipline outlived the doctrine that produced it. Karl Marx had derived the spirit from the material conditions; Weber runs the arrow the other way for one stretch of the road and spends the rest of his life denying he ever said it runs only that way.
stops.quote: In Baxter's view the care for external goods should only lie on the shoulders of the 'saint like a light cloak, which can be thrown aside at any moment.' But fate decreed that the cloak should become an iron cage.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 5; the inner phrase is Weber quoting Richard Baxter, and 'iron cage' is Parsons's contested rendering of stahlhartes Gehäuse
suggested_refs: Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, vols. 20 and 21 (1904-1905)
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism'

stops.name: Heidelberg, Russian learned in a season
stops.date_confidence: the two Russian essays are attested to 1905; no month is given
stops.campa: Revolution breaks out in Russia and Weber, who does not read the language, learns it inside a few months, well enough to follow the newspapers, and produces two long essays on the prospects of constitutional liberty there. His conclusion is unwelcome to every party: Russian liberalism has arrived too late, in a country whose economic development will manufacture bureaucracy faster than it manufactures citizens. He is describing, without naming it, a mechanism he expects to reach Germany on the same schedule.
suggested_refs: Zur Lage der bürgerlichen Demokratie in Russland (1906) and its companion essay

stops.name: Heidelberg, the inheritance
stops.date_confidence: the inheritance is attested to 1907; no month is given
stops.campa: A legacy settles the question of money permanently. He will never again need a salaried chair and does not take one for twelve years. What this buys is a kind of scholarship the German university system does not otherwise permit: no lectures, no examinations, no faculty politics, and a working day arranged entirely around a body that still cannot be pushed hard. The Economic Ethics of the World Religions and the Grundriss manuscript both belong to that condition and neither would exist without it.
suggested_refs: The 1907 legacy and the economics of the German Privatgelehrter

stops.name: Venice, the Piazza San Marco
stops.date_confidence: the Venice journey is attested to 1909; no month is given
stops.campa: He travels to Venice with Marianne, with Else von Richthofen and with the pianist Mina Tobler. In the same year he helps found the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Soziologie and becomes its first treasurer, a post he resigns in 1912 after quarrelling over whether a scholarly society may hold political opinions. He argues that it may not. The same twelve months hold a discipline formally constituted in Germany and a private life beginning to arrange itself in ways the biographies handle carefully.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Soziologie, 1909, and the Werturteilsstreit

stops.name: Heidelberg, the Fallensteinvilla and the Sunday circle
stops.date_confidence: the move is attested to 1910; no month is given, and the circle is dated from the move rather than from the 1896 appointment as some summaries have it
stops.campa: The Webers move into his grandparents' villa at Ziegelhäuser Landstraße 17, above the Neckar, and the house becomes the address of the circle: Jellinek, Troeltsch, Simmel when he visits, later Jaspers and Lukács, a Sunday afternoon that runs on for years and outlasts most of the university appointments in the room. In 1911 the relationship with Mina Tobler begins, and the villa holds that too, the same rooms doing double duty as seminar and confidence.
suggested_refs: The Fallensteinsche Villa, Ziegelhäuser Landstraße 17, Heidelberg, and the Sonntagsjour
sources: Nominatim geocoding of Ziegelhäuser Landstraße 17 (correcting a pool figure on the wrong bank of the Neckar)

stops.name: Ascona, Monte Verità
stops.date_confidence: the 1913 holiday is attested to the year; no month is given
stops.campa: Above Ascona, on a hill bought by vegetarians, a colony of anarchists, nudists, theosophists, dancers and psychoanalysts is running an experiment in living without the discipline Weber has spent nine years anatomizing. He comes on holiday, and he argues. He takes the place seriously as evidence rather than as scandal: a deliberate attempt to found an ethic on eros instead of on vocation, staged on a Swiss hillside by people who have in several cases read him. The commune and the iron cage are one question asked from opposite ends.
stops.quote: The earning of more and more money, combined with the strict avoidance of all spontaneous enjoyment of life, is above all completely devoid of any eudaemonistic, not to say hedonistic, admixture.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 2
suggested_refs: Monte Verità above Ascona and the Lebensreform colonies before 1914

stops.name: Ascona, the last spring
stops.date_confidence: the spring 1914 holiday is attested; no day is given
stops.campa: He returns in April. Four months later the mobilization orders go out, and this way of spending a spring ends for everyone on the hill and for most of Europe. Nothing in the reachable record suggests he sees it coming. The last documented holiday of Max Weber's life is spent among people who believe the century is about to grow gentler, in a country that will stay neutral, a short distance from borders that are about to matter enormously. He is fifty, and for the first time since 1898 he is in something like working health.
suggested_refs: Weber's second Ascona stay, spring 1914

stops.name: Heidelberg, the reserve officer and the hospitals
stops.date_confidence: the service begins in August 1914 and runs to the end of 1915; the day of commissioning is not given
stops.campa: He volunteers, is commissioned as a reserve officer, and is handed the district's military hospitals to organize: beds, supplies, staff, discharge papers, the whole apparatus. For a year and a half the theorist of bureaucratic administration administers. He supports the war at the outset, in the terms of his Freiburg address, and turns against the Kaiser's conduct of it well before most of his colleagues do. In 1915 his younger brother Karl is killed on the Eastern Front near Brest-Litovsk.
stops.quote: Bureaucracy has a "rational" character: rules, means, ends, and matter-of-factness dominate its bearing.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, 'Bureaucracy,' in H. H. Gerth and C. Wright Mills, From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology (1946), p. 244; the German behind it is Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft ch. XI, drafted in these years
suggested_refs: The Heidelberg reserve hospital administration, 1914-1915

stops.name: Burg Lauenstein, the conference in the Frankenwald
stops.date_confidence: the conferences are attested to 1917 and Weber is photographed in discussion in May of that year; the exact session dates are not given
stops.campa: In a castle on a wooded ridge in Upper Franconia a publisher gathers intellectuals to argue about what German culture should become after a war that is visibly being lost. The younger men want a leader, a renewal, a return of meaning. Weber tells them the world has been disenchanted, that no conference can re-enchant it, and that anyone who cannot bear this should go back to the churches, which will take him in without reproach. He is not thanked. The photograph of the session survives; he is the one leaning forward.
stops.quote: The rosy blush of its laughing heir, the Enlightenment, seems also to be irretrievably fading, and the idea of duty in one's calling prowls about in our lives like the ghost of dead religious beliefs.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 5
suggested_refs: The Lauensteiner Kulturtagungen of 1917, convened by Eugen Diederichs
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Burg Lauenstein' (coordinate 50°30′47.9″N 11°22′11″E, correcting a pool figure 7 km southeast)

stops.name: Munich, Science as a Vocation
stops.date_confidence: the lecture is attested to November 1917; no day is given, and the pin marks Munich rather than the hall, which the reachable sources do not name
stops.campa: He speaks to students of the Freistudentischer Bund, not from any chair, and tells them what an academic life is actually made of: chance, drudgery, and specialization so narrow that a scholar may hope to be right about one thing. Science cannot tell anyone how to live. The disenchantment of the world is the price of knowing how it works, and the lecture refuses, at length and without consolation, to pretend otherwise. They have come expecting a prophet and are told precisely that prophets are what a lecture hall cannot supply.
suggested_refs: Wissenschaft als Beruf, Munich, November 1917, published 1919
sources: [R] the venue is unlocated; the coordinate is the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität used as a Munich city marker

stops.name: Vienna, the return to the lecture hall
stops.date_confidence: the summer semester of 1918 is attested; the month is inferred from the Austrian semester calendar
stops.campa: For the first time in twenty years he holds a regular teaching post, a summer semester at Vienna, and the hall is full. The course is on economy and society, delivered as a positive critique of the materialist conception of history. He finds that he can still do it. He declines the offer to stay. The empire he is lecturing inside has a few months left to run; his audience contains men who will spend their careers arguing about whether he was right, in successor states that do not yet exist.
suggested_refs: The Vienna summer semester of 1918 and the lecture course Eine positive Kritik der materialistischen Geschichtsauffassung

stops.name: Munich, Politics as a Vocation
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Three weeks after his failed candidacy for the National Assembly, in a city where the revolution has not yet decided what it is, he speaks to the free students again. Politics is not conviction, he tells them, but responsibility for consequences, exercised by men who handle power and cannot keep clean hands. The state is the human community claiming the monopoly of legitimate physical force within a territory. The charismatic type he names here will be read, within three years, against the first of the century's marches on a capital.
stops.quote: Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards. It takes both passion and perspective.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, 'Politics as a Vocation,' in H. H. Gerth and C. Wright Mills, From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology (1946), p. 128; the German is 'Die Politik bedeutet ein starkes langsames Bohren von harten Brettern mit Leidenschaft und Augenmass zugleich'
suggested_refs: Politik als Beruf, Munich, 28 January 1919, delivered to the Freistudentischer Bund
sources: [R] the venue is unlocated; the coordinate is the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität used as a Munich city marker

stops.name: Versailles, the German delegation
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He goes to Versailles with the German delegation as an adviser, having already sat on the committee drafting the constitution at Weimar and helped found the German Democratic Party. The terms are presented rather than negotiated. He argues against signing, is overruled, and comes home knowing the republic he helped design will carry this document as a founding wound. His typology of legitimate domination, rational-legal, traditional and charismatic, is the last major work of theory he completes before the disease that will kill him within the year.
stops.quote: The state is a relation of men dominating men, a relation supported by means of legitimate (i.e. considered to be legitimate) violence.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Max Weber, 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919); widely cited, but not verified against any fetched text in the research for this file, and carried here as [R]
suggested_refs: The German delegation at Versailles, May 1919, and Weber's memorandum on war guilt

stops.name: Munich, the chair at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is attested to 1919; he begins lecturing in the summer semester, after returning from the Versailles delegation in May, and no day is given
stops.campa: At fifty-five he takes a salaried chair again, succeeding Lujo Brentano, and lectures on economic history to halls that will not hold the audience. He has no manuscript for the course; the students take it down, and in 1923 Siegmund Hellmann and Melchior Palyi assemble their notebooks into the volume published as General Economic History. It is the only complete book of his to reach print in a form he never wrote. Munich in these months is under the guns of the Freikorps, and he teaches through it.
suggested_refs: Wirtschaftsgeschichte (1923), from the Munich lecture transcripts

stops.name: Munich-Schwabing, the apartment on the Seestraße
stops.date_confidence: the residence is attested to the Munich years, 1919-1920; no month of arrival is given
stops.campa: The Webers take rooms at Seestraße 3c in Schwabing, the quarter of painters and cafés, a district still recovering from the street fighting of the Bavarian Soviet Republic that spring. Marianne runs the household, which from April 1920 includes the four children of his sister Lili Schäfer, who has taken her own life. On the desk lies the unfinished Grundriss manuscript he has been at since 1909, alongside the lecture notes for Economy and Society, both still incomplete when the year runs out.
suggested_refs: The Weber apartment at Seestraße 3c, Munich-Schwabing
sources: Nominatim geocoding of Seestraße 3, Alt-Schwabing (correcting two pool figures several hundred metres northwest)

stops.name: Munich-Schwabing, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He tells his students he has a cold. Within days it is pneumonia, in the tail of the influenza pandemic, and on the fourteenth of June he dies in the Schwabing apartment at fifty-six. The Grundriss is unfinished and will stay unfinished; the comparative studies of the world religions break off in the middle of the third civilization. He has held a salaried chair for fourteen months out of the previous twenty-three years. The reachable sources give the date and the cause and nothing of the hour.
suggested_refs: The death notice of 14 June 1920 and the state of the Grundriss manuscript at that date

stops.name: Munich, the Ostfriedhof
stops.date_confidence: the funeral and cremation are attested to June 1920; no reachable source gives the day, so the date of death is carried forward
stops.campa: The funeral is secular, without clergy, at Munich's eastern cemetery in Obergiesing, and Marianne speaks the eulogy. Eduard Baumgarten and Karl Loewenstein, his students, and Lujo Brentano, whose chair he had taken, are recorded among those present. The body is cremated there. Two sources consulted disagreed about where the Ostfriedhof stands, by a kilometre and a half; the cemetery's own coordinate is used here, and the disagreement is recorded rather than smoothed away.
suggested_refs: The Ostfriedhof crematorium, Munich-Obergiesing

stops.name: Heidelberg, the urn in Abteilung E
stops.date_confidence: the interment is attested to 1921; no month or day is given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A year after the death the urn is carried up to the Bergfriedhof on the slope above Heidelberg and set in section E. Tradition puts a thousand mourners on the path; no reachable source counts them, and the figure is repeated rather than attested. He is back in the town where he matriculated in 1882, took Knies's chair in 1896, broke down in 1898 and wrote everything afterwards. It is about two kilometres from the villa on the Ziegelhäuser Landstraße where the circle used to meet.
suggested_refs: Bergfriedhof Heidelberg, Abteilung E, the Weber grave
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Bergfriedhof (Heidelberg)', coordinate 49.3972 / 8.6903 (correcting two pool figures up to 800 m north)

stops.name: Heidelberg, the books Marianne assembles
stops.date_confidence: the Wissenschaftslehre appears in 1922 and Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft across 1921-1922; January 1922 is a placeholder for the editorial years
stops.campa: From the villa she edits. Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft is cut, ordered and published out of the unfinished Grundriss across 1921 and 1922; the second and third volumes of the essays on the sociology of religion follow, and the Wissenschaftslehre in 1922, and the biography in 1926. He had assembled the first religion volume himself before he died, which is a distinction the summaries usually lose. Every decision about what the century will call Max Weber's system is taken at this desk.
suggested_refs: Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft (1921-1922), ed. Marianne Weber, in the Grundriss der Sozialökonomik

stops.name: Heidelberg, the second name on the stone
stops.date_confidence: Marianne Weber's death is attested to 1954; the reachable sources give the year and the shared grave, not the day of burial
stops.campa: Marianne Weber dies at eighty-four and is buried in the same grave. The Bergfriedhof register lists them together in Abteilung E: Max Weber 1864-1920, Marianne Weber geborene Schnitger 1870-1954. Thirty-four years separate the two dates. In that interval she makes the corpus, defends it under a regime that has no use for either of them, and puts a second name on a stone that had been one man's alone. The iron cage is Parsons's phrase, not Weber's; the shell as hard as steel is closer.
stops.quote: Specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart; this nullity imagines that it has attained a level of civilization never before achieved.
stops.quote_source: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons, ch. 5, closing paragraph
suggested_refs: The Max Weber-Gesamtausgabe, the critical edition of works and correspondence
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism'
